question: In maternal-fetal care, who are the two main patients the midwife and doctor look after?

options.A: The obstetrician and the labor ward midwife
options.B: The primary caregiver and the family head
options.C: The pregnant woman and the developing fetus
options.D: The neonate and the pediatric specialist

explanation: Maternal-fetal medicine focuses simultaneously on the health and clinical needs of both the mother and the unborn child. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why has the management of high-risk pregnancies improved so much in modern hospitals?

options.A: Midwives no longer manage high-risk cases without direct consultant supervision
options.B: Fetal complications are universally prevented by standard nutritional supplements
options.C: Routine antenatal clinics have completely eliminated the need for surgical rescue
options.D: Advanced clinical treatments can now help treat complex conditions before birth

explanation: Modern medical and surgical advancements allow clinicians to treat conditions inside the womb that previously had very poor outcomes. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which condition is a common reason for giving a baby a blood transfusion while still inside the womb?
explanation: Intra-uterine blood transfusions are primarily given to correct severe fetal anemia caused by conditions like Rhesus incompatibility or viral infections. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the main goal of laser surgery inside the womb for twins who share a placenta?

options.A: To seal shared placental blood vessels causing twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
options.B: To prevent the development of congenital heart defects in both fetuses
options.C: To accelerate lung maturity before planned preterm delivery
options.D: To treat severe maternal hypertension during the second trimester

explanation: Fetoscopic laser ablation targets and interrupts the abnormal vascular connections on the placenta that cause unequal blood sharing between twins. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is a major risk that doctors and midwives must watch out for when planning surgery inside the womb?

options.A: Triggering early labor through the early breaking of the water bag
options.B: Causing permanent postpartum depression in the biological father
options.C: Increasing the incidence of post-term pregnancies significantly
options.D: Permanently stopping the normal maternal menstrual cycle

explanation: Uterine manipulation during fetal surgery frequently triggers premature labor or rupture of membranes, posing serious risks to the baby. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h3)

question: What should be the main factor when deciding to perform an advanced surgery on an unborn baby?

options.A: The availability of high-resolution cameras in the operating theatre
options.B: Standard hospital protocols requiring surgery for all twin gestations
options.C: The personal preference of the surgical team performing the operation
options.D: Proven long-term benefits for the baby outweighing the immediate risks of the surgery

explanation: Clinicians must always ensure that the expected advantages to the newborn clearly justify the surgical risks imposed on the mother and fetus. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a typical complication a mother might face from complex high-risk surgeries?
explanation: Pulmonary valve dysplasia is a congenital heart defect, not a surgical complication caused by maternal-fetal interventions. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h4)

question: If a mother develops an infection inside her womb after an invasive procedure, what has most likely happened?

options.A: Acute maternal iron deficiency anemia triggered by intraoperative blood loss
options.B: Sudden hormonal changes leading to sterile inflammation of the womb muscle
options.C: Rapid closure of the fetal heart vessel causing secondary placental failure
options.D: Bacteria entered the amniotic cavity because the bag of waters was breached

explanation: Invasive procedures breach the protective barriers of the amniotic sac, allowing bacteria to enter and cause intra-amniotic infection. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why can just looking at newborn survival rates after surgery give an incomplete picture of success?

options.A: They often do not show if the baby will have long-term breathing or brain challenges
options.B: They are usually calculated by hospital administrators rather than pediatricians
options.C: They only include babies who were delivered via spontaneous vaginal birth
options.D: They automatically exclude twins and higher-order multiple pregnancies

explanation: Surviving the newborn period does not guarantee a healthy childhood, as many infants suffer lifelong disabilities from birth trauma or prematurity. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h5)

question: At what ages are high-risk babies usually checked thoroughly for long-term health and development?

options.B: At two and five years of age
options.C: At six weeks and three months

explanation: Long-term follow-up assessments at two and five years help clinicians detect chronic neurological, speech, and motor delays. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h5)

question: What creates a difficult ethical challenge when a pregnant woman refuses treatment during severe fetal distress?

options.A: The mother's right to refuse treatment conflicting with efforts to save her baby
options.B: The absolute refusal of pediatricians to participate in emergency cesarean sections
options.C: The strict legal requirement for universal free healthcare in all public hospitals
options.D: The impossibility of getting informed consent from a conscious laboring woman

explanation: Because the fetus resides inside the mother, her legal autonomy to accept or decline procedures directly impacts the survival chances of the unborn child. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h6)

question: What financial factor often makes emergency obstetric decisions harder in many Nigerian hospitals?

options.A: Patients having to pay out-of-pocket for their care
options.B: The complete absence of trained midwives in teaching hospitals
options.C: Universal legislative bans on performing cesarean section deliveries
options.D: The mandatory requirement for paternal consent in all medical procedures

explanation: Lack of immediate funds for drugs, blood, and surgery often delays critical interventions in settings relying heavily on out-of-pocket payments. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h6)

question: A patient with a suspected placental abruption is waiting for surgery because blood is delayed. What should the midwife do right away?

options.A: Wait passively until the relatives find money without checking on the patient
options.B: Give pain relief by mouth and tell the patient to walk around the ward
options.C: Discharge the patient against medical advice since immediate surgery is clearly impossible
options.D: Keep a close watch on vital signs, follow up on the blood bank, and get ready for an emergency

explanation: Midwives must maintain rigorous surveillance and actively chase required resources while keeping the patient stable for imminent theater transfer. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why is it helpful for the medical team to meet and review a complicated case after it happens?

options.A: To file mandatory legal reports against the hospital management board
options.B: To stop writing standard clinical notes in the ward register
options.C: To punish junior staff members directly responsible for clinical errors
options.D: To spot system problems and make care safer for future patients

explanation: Reviewing cases as a team helps identify bottlenecks, communication gaps, and infrastructural failures to prevent similar adverse outcomes later. [learn more](BMP226_U1_T5#BMP226_U1_T5_h7)
